title: Judging the Judges: Confidence and Disagreement in Rubrics as Rewards

paper.title: Judging the Judges: Confidence and Disagreement in Rubrics as Rewards
paper.abstract: Abstract Rubrics as Rewards (RaR) extends reinforcement learning to non-verifiable domains by using an LLM judge to score responses against a structured rubric. Prior work has focused on improving the rubric or strengthening the single judge, with comparatively little attention to how different single or multiple judges might be used during RaR training. We first show that judge identity alone produces a substantial spread in scores when training Qwen3-4B-Base on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science across five frontier and open-weight judges. Building on this, we propose RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a novel judge ensemble strategy for RaR with two mechanisms: a soft-Likert reward that uses judge logprobs to weight more confident judges more heavily, and a drop-on-disagreement mask that excludes high-disagreement rollouts from the GRPO update. We find that this design is critical: while a naive average of judge scores fails to outperform the best single judge, RaRE outperforms every single-judge RaR variant on both HealthBench and GPQA Diamond, with per-theme analysis showing that it inherits the complementary strengths of its constituent judges. Our findings establish judge ensembling as a compelling axis for improving RaR. 1 1 1 Project page: https://anneharrington.github.io/judging-the-judges/

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Rubrics as Rewards (RaR; Gunjal et al., 2025 ) is increasingly used in LLM post-training for learning on non-verifiable domains. Unlike Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which is standard for math and code ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , RaR enables training in more realistic settings where response quality might depend on multiple criteria that are not easily checked (such as completeness, style, and safety). RaR consists of two components: a structured, instance-specific rubric that encodes relevant criteria, and an LLM judge that scores each rollout against the rubric to produce a scalar reward. Following its success, subsequent work has explored in depth how to improve rubrics themselves; these include better offline construction ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , checklist-style scaffolding during rollouts ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and online rubric updates ( Rezaei et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . While the effect of the judge has been studied extensively at evaluation time, including work on judge ensembles ( Verga et al., 2024 ; Chan et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) , comparatively the impact of the judge during RaR training has been under-explored. To fill this gap, we evaluate the role of the judge model during RaR training more broadly. We train Qwen3-4B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science with the same strategy and rubrics as Gunjal et al. (2025) across 5 open and closed weight judging models. We show that varying judge identity alone in RaR produces a substantial spread in scores across both domains. Using our insights on the effect of the single judge model, we then develop RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a novel ensemble strategy to improve RaR. Rather than taking a naive average of judge scores, which we show fails to outperform the best single judge, RaRE targets two distinct sources of uncertainty. First, we introduce a soft-Likert reward to leverage intra-judge confidence: we use each judge’s logprobs to weight more confident judges more heavily in the ensemble. Second, we incorporate a drop-on-disagreement mask to leverage inter-judge disagreement: we exclude rollouts on which judges strongly disagree from the GRPO update. The two mechanisms can be used independently or composed. We validate RaRE on an ensemble of two judges, testing on the medicine and science domains using HealthBench ( Arora et al., 2025 ) and GPQA Diamond ( Rein et al., 2023 ) respectively. We find that our best RaRE configuration outperforms every single-judge RaR variant in both domains (0.364 vs. 0.339 best single judge on HealthBench; 0.412 vs. 0.406 best single judge on GPQA Diamond). Examining results by HealthBench theme, we find that RaRE consistently inherits the strengths of its judges, winning on all seven themes. Figure 1: Overview of RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), instantiated with two judges. (1) Inputs: the user prompt, rubric, and a model rollout sampled from the policy (Qwen3-4B-Base) are passed to the judges. (2) Two-judge ensemble: we use an ensemble of two diverse LLM judges (selected from a pool of frontier and open-weight models). Each judge scores the rollout against the rubric on a 1–5 Likert scale, and we read its top-5 logprobs to recover an expected rating E i E_{i} and a per-judge confidence C i C_{i} . (3) Reward construction: our soft-Likert reward (A) combines the two expected ratings into a single scalar by weighting each judge by its inverse-variance confidence. Our drop-on-disagreement mask (B) excludes rollouts where the two judges’ expected ratings differ by more than τ ⋅ ( 5 − 1 ) \tau\cdot(5-1) from the GRPO update. Together, our results suggest that the judge model is a major design choice in RaR, and that small ensembles with the right aggregation can deliver a stronger training signal than any single judge. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. A study of the judge in RaR training across five frontier and open-weight judges on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science, showing that judge identity alone substantially shifts policy quality. 2. RaRE, a novel ensemble method for RaR with two composable mechanisms: a soft-Likert reward that reads judge logprobs to recover confidence-weighted ratings, and a drop-on-disagreement mask that excludes high-disagreement rollouts from the GRPO update. 3. Empirical results showing that RaRE outperforms single-judge RaR variants in both medicine and science, with per-theme analysis revealing that it inherits complementary strengths of its judges, unlike a naive ensemble approach.

sections.heading: RL with verifiable rewards.
sections.text: Recent gains on math and code use deterministic checks (e.g., calculators, compilers) as the reward signal ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , typically optimized with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . These checks do not exist for open-ended domains such as medical or scientific ( Su et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Rubric-based rewards.
sections.text: Rubrics-as-Rewards ( Gunjal et al., 2025 ) and similar work ( Viswanathan et al., 2026 ) replace the binary verifier with an LLM judge that scores a candidate against a structured rubric, converting a fuzzy preference target into a scalar reward. Subsequent work has focused almost entirely on the rubric side: better offline construction ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , checklist-style scaffolding during rollouts ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , online rubric updates ( Rezaei et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , and causally grounded rubrics for robust reward modeling ( Srivastava et al., 2026 ) . Concurrent work ( Mahmoud et al., 2026 ) also uses multiple judges in the RaR setting, but as a multi-judge evaluation panel for detecting reward hacking, while RaRE uses the judge ensemble as the training signal itself. Across these works, the training judge model is consistently treated as a fixed implementation detail, usually a single model. Our work holds the rubric fixed and treats the judge itself as the design variable, complementary to all of the above.

sections.heading: LLM-as-a-judge and verification.
sections.text: LLM-as-a-judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) has become the dominant evaluation paradigm, with growing emphasis on structured or rubric-conditioned grading ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Hashemi et al., 2024 ) . Recent reliability studies ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ; Kwok et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) show that single judges exhibit substantial position bias, length bias, and inter-seed variance. Our results in § 4.2 extend this diagnosis from evaluation to optimization: judge choice meaningfully affects the trained policy even with a fixed rubric.

sections.heading: Judge ensembles.
sections.text: The closest prior work is Panel-of-LLM-evaluators ( Verga et al., 2024 ) , which mean-pools or majority-votes across a panel of smaller judges and shows that the panel outperforms a single large judge on evaluation while reducing intra-model bias. ChatEval ( Chan et al., 2024 ) explores a debate-based variant, and similar work ( Feng et al., 2025 ) finds that panel-based judging improves preference consistency. To our knowledge, all of this literature treats judge ensembles as an evaluation-time mechanism. RaRE instead uses a judge ensemble inside the RL training loop as the reward signal, with mechanisms (§ 3.1.2 , § 3.1.3 ) that use inter-judge spread as part of the training signal rather than only as a diagnostic.

sections.heading: 3.1 Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles
sections.text: We propose RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), which replaces the single training judge with an ensemble of K K judges. We first describe the naive ensemble baseline (§ 3.1.1 ), then RaRE’s two composable mechanisms: the soft-Likert reward (§ 3.1.2 ) and the drop-on-disagreement mask (§ 3.1.3 ).

(2) This averages out idiosyncratic per-judge bias while keeping the training pipeline unchanged.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Soft-Likert reward via judge logprobs
sections.text: The naive ensemble (§ 3.1.1 ) treats each judge’s rating as a single integer, discarding the judge’s confidence in that rating. We propose a soft-Likert reward that recovers confidence from the judge’s output distribution and uses it both as a continuous reward and as a weight for ensemble aggregation.

sections.heading: Policy and reference models.
sections.text: Our trainable policy is Qwen3-4B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) ; we report Qwen3-4B as a tuned reference throughout.

sections.heading: Judges.
sections.text: Five candidate single-judge configurations span proprietary, open-weight, and small-model regimes: gpt-4o-mini ( OpenAI, 2024 ) , DeepSeek-V3.1 ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ) , Gemini-2.5-flash-lite ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-235B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and gpt-oss-120b ( OpenAI et al., 2025 ) . All judges share the same rubric and same Likert-rating prompt template (Appendix J ). Soft-Likert (Eq. 7 ) requires the endpoint to return top_logprobs . We queried logprobs for the two judges used in our soft-Likert ensemble experiments (gpt-4o-mini and DeepSeek-V3.1); Gemini does not expose this in its API. All judges were run with no thinking or low effort reasoning when applicable.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: We train on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science ( Gunjal et al., 2025 ) with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) using G = 8 G{=}8 generations per prompt and per-group reward normalization. Full hyperparameters stated in Appendix P . Headline numbers use full-parameter fine-tuning; we report a brief LoRA comparison in the length-hacking discussion below.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate on the English-only subset of HealthBench for medicine, using gpt-4o-mini as the eval judge ( Arora et al., 2025 ) , and GPQA Diamond for science ( Rein et al., 2023 ) , with max completion tokens capped at 8192 (responses are truncated past this). Throughout, we refer to the English-only subset simply as HealthBench. Furthermore, we split GPQA Diamond into disjoint 50/50 validation/test splits for purposes of hyperparameter tuning, with results reported on the test split. For some ablations, we evaluate on a subset of 1,000 prompts (randomly sampled, stratified by theme) which we refer to as the HealthBench 1K subset (with max completion tokens capped at 1024). We report the mean HealthBench/GPQA Diamond score (henceforth “score”) across prompts. For GPQA Diamond, we train models on 5 seeds and report the mean score and 95% confidence intervals. HealthBench provides bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals, stated in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 4.2 Single-Judge RaR is Sensitive to Judge
sections.text: Figure 2 compares RaR-trained Qwen3-4B-Base under five different judges, all sharing the same rubric (training dynamics in Fig. 9 ). The spread across judges ( 0.296 0.296 – 0.339 0.339 on English-only HealthBench, ∼ \sim 4.3 pp) is comparable to the gap between RL and the untrained base ( 0.257 0.257 ). Furthermore, the best single-judge RaR ( 0.339 0.339 ) comfortably exceeds Qwen3-4B ( 0.307 0.307 ), while the worst single-judge RaR ( 0.296 0.296 ) does worse than Qwen3-4B. A similar sensitivity to judge choice is observed on GPQA Diamond (Figure 3 ), where the single-judge spread is 0.345 0.345 – 0.406 0.406 . Judge identity therefore has large effects on RaR outcomes under fixed rubric, with spread comparable to the gap between RL and the untrained base. This motivates treating judge selection as a key design variable. sections.text: We break down performance of selected judges by HealthBench theme (Figure 4 , showing each judge’s delta in mean reward vs. the Qwen3-4B-Base baseline) and find that no single judge dominates; different judges have complementary strengths across themes. sections.heading: Length hacking.
sections.text: Reward models and LLM judges have been shown to favor longer responses ( Singhal et al., 2023 ; Saito et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . In our experiments, Table 2 shows that RaR training under several judges inflates response length dramatically. 97% of gpt-oss-120b’s post-training responses hit a 4k-character ( ∼ \sim 1024-token) cap vs. ∼ \sim 4% for the untrained Qwen3-4B-Base. We explore two interventions that partially recover this: (i) an explicit length penalty during training ( 4o-mini_lenpen ), which keeps responses short with no reward loss; (ii) LoRA fine-tuning ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , which we find empirically dampens the length expansion (mini-LoRA: 0.295 0.295 reward, 1,058 1{,}058 mean characters vs. full-FT mini: 0.296 0.296 reward, 2,930 2{,}930 mean characters). The LoRA dampening generalizes to RaRE: Gem+DS (mean+drop) scores 0.330 0.330 under full-FT vs. 0.295 0.295 under LoRA, a ∼ \sim 3 pp cost for substantially shorter outputs and lower training compute (Appendix M ). We use full-FT for headline numbers, but the gap is small enough that LoRA remains a useful tradeoff. sections.heading: 4.3 RaRE Outperforms Single-Judge RaR
sections.text: Based on the per-theme complementarity in Figure 4 , we instantiate RaRE with two judges. We use two judge pairs in our experiments: Gemini-2.5-flash-lite with DeepSeek-V3.1 ( Gem+DS ) for hard-Likert configurations, and DeepSeek-V3.1 with GPT-4o-mini ( DS+Mini ) for soft-Likert configurations, since both endpoints of the latter pair expose the token-level logprobs that soft-Likert requires. Each pair was chosen so that the two judges differ in vendor, scale, and training data. We evaluate the three ensemble strategies from § 3 (naive mean, soft-Likert, drop-on-disagreement) and their composition. We sweep RaRE’s drop-on-disagreement parameter τ \tau and refer to the best settings per ensemble and dataset simply as drop (see Tables 3 and 4 ). Figures 2 and 3 report ensemble results on HealthBench and GPQA Diamond. The HealthBench score from ensembling the naive mean of Gemini and DeepSeek’s integer ratings (0.307) sits between the two constituent judges (0.296 Gemini, 0.338 DeepSeek). Naive averaging alone does not outperform single judges; the gains we report from RaRE below come from filtering or reweighting, not averaging. Adding drop-on-disagreement (mean + drop) to the Gemini+DeepSeek naive mean (0.347) lifts the score + 0.8 +0.8 pp above the best single judge by filtering the ∼ \sim 5% of rollouts where the two judges disagree most. Soft-Likert on DeepSeek+GPT-4o-mini without drop (0.330) slightly hurts performance compared to the constituent judges: low-confidence disagreement rollouts get down-weighted but not removed, and their residual contribution may distort the GRPO advantage estimate. Composing soft-Likert with drop on the same pair ( 0.364 \mathbf{0.364} ) zeroes the high-disagreement rollouts and lets the soft-Likert reward on the rest become the strongest signal we have, exceeding the best single judge by + 2.5 +2.5 pp. The two mechanisms therefore target different uncertainty sources and compose. On GPQA Diamond, we see that ensembling Gemini+DeepSeek naive mean (0.363) also sits close to the two constituent judges (0.360 Gemini, 0.345 DeepSeek). sections.heading: Complementary judge strengths.
sections.text: Figure 4 shows that single judges win on disjoint themes on HealthBench: DeepSeek wins communication , context_seeking , emergency_referrals , and global_health ; GPT-4o-mini wins complex_responses , data_tasks , and hedging . Furthermore, our best RaRE configuration (soft + drop on DeepSeek+GPT-4o-mini) combines the strengths of its two constituent judges and achieves the best results in each theme across the board. RaRE thus inherits, rather than averages out, the constituent judges’ theme-level strengths. In Appendix Figure 6 , we similarly report per-topic accuracy on GPQA Diamond, which demonstrates the qualities of different judges.

sections.text: Our strongest configuration combines soft-Likert with a disagreement threshold of τ = 0.30 \tau{=}0.30 on medicine and τ = 0.40 \tau{=}0.40 on science. sections.heading: Judge choice matters in RaR.
sections.text: Varying the judge under a fixed rubric produces a ∼ \sim 4.3 pp spread in HealthBench score across five judges. This spread is greater than the gap between Qwen3-4B-Base and the lowest single-judge RaR run. Prior RaR work has focused almost exclusively on improving the rubric, treating the judge as fixed. Our results suggest that the judge side carries comparable signal and deserves comparable attention.

sections.heading: Ensembles win by combining complementary judges, not by averaging.
sections.text: We might expect a judge ensemble to smooth out variance from any single judge, with the ensemble converging toward the strongest judge. We do not find this. RaRE consistently improves on HealthBench themes beyond either of its two judges individually (Figure 4 ), suggesting that the gain comes from combining the judges’ non-overlapping strengths, rather than from selecting the stronger judge. Naive averaging does not extract this gain: the mean of judges’ ratings averages their individual scores and does not outperform the best single judge. The gain only appears once we filter high-disagreement rollouts.

sections.heading: Disagreement filtering is the most impactful mechanism.
sections.text: Across our ablations, the drop-on-disagreement mask contributes the most. Adding it to the naive Gemini+DeepSeek mean ensemble lifts the score by + 4.0 +4.0 pp (0.307 to 0.347); removing it from the DeepSeek+4o-mini soft+drop configuration costs 3.4 3.4 pp (0.364 to 0.330). The soft-Likert reward provides additional gain when composed with the mask, but on its own does not outperform the best single judge on HealthBench. The broader LLM-as-a-verifier literature ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ; Kwok et al., 2026 ) reports a similar finding in the evaluation setting, where explicit disagreement filtering matters more than the choice of any single judge. Our results extend this from evaluation to training.

sections.heading: Relation to concurrent and complementary work.
sections.text: Two recent directions are complementary to ours. Online rubric updates ( Rezaei et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) reduce reward-signal variance by improving rubric content during training; we reduce it by improving judge aggregation. The two operate on different parts of the RaR pipeline and should compose, though we leave that combination to future work. Concurrent work by Mahmoud et al. (2026) also uses multiple judges in the RaR setting, but in the opposite direction: they train against a single verifier and use a cross-family panel of three frontier judges to diagnose reward hacking, while we use multiple judges to produce the training signal. The two contributions are independent and could be combined, with RaRE serving as the training-time signal and their panel as the evaluation-time check.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We proposed RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), combining a soft-Likert confidence-aggregation reward with a drop-on-disagreement mask, which outperforms every single-judge RaR variant on both HealthBench and GPQA-Diamond. Our results suggest RaRE’s gains arise from combining complementary judge strengths through confidence and disagreement aggregation.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Due to limited compute, our experiments are restricted to a single base policy (Qwen3-4B-Base) evaluated on two domains: HealthBench (medicine) and GPQA Diamond (science), so our findings may not transfer to other policy families, model scales, or other domains. We mitigate this with per-theme and per-category breakdowns and extensive ablations, but broader validation is left to future work. We evaluate HealthBench with GPT-4o-mini, following the convention established by Arora et al. (2025) and Gunjal et al. (2025) , which may introduce evaluation-judge bias since it is also used as a training judge. To test whether this overlap affects our results, we regrade policy responses with GLM-5.3-Flash, a judge from a different model family (Appendix D ). Relative rankings remain similar, and RaRE ranks first under both judges. A larger multi-judge evaluation panel, such as the one used by Mahmoud et al. (2026) , would provide additional robustness against evaluation-judge bias; our GPQA Diamond results, which use verifier-style evaluation rather than an LLM judge, partially address this concern. RaRE’s improvement on GPQA Diamond compared to single-judge RaR is not statistically significant across 5 training seeds. Running additional seeds could help tighten confidence intervals and allow for a more definitive comparison, which we leave to future work due to compute constraints. When applying RaRE’s drop-on-disagreement mask, we discard the dropped rollouts entirely rather than extracting any partial signal from them. Initial exploratory attempts in this direction (Appendix O ) did not yield any improvement over our baseline methods, but further exploration is left to future work. Finally, RaRE depends on inter-judge disagreement as a signal. When judges largely agree, RaRE provides little additional signal beyond a single judge; a more diverse judge pool could expand the regime where ensembling helps.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Our work studies how judge selection and judge ensembling affect rubric-based RL training, with the goal of making the reward signal more reliable. Because the resulting policies are trained against LLM-judge rewards, they inherit biases of the judges used: RaRE reduces idiosyncratic per-judge bias but does not eliminate biases shared across judges, and the drop-on-disagreement filter removes precisely those rollouts where judges disagree most, which could exclude cases where a single judge correctly flags a safety-relevant issue that others miss. We therefore encourage practitioners who deploy ensemble-trained policies, particularly in health or scientific contexts, to audit them separately for these biases rather than treat ensembling as a substitute for evaluation, and we treat the models in this work as research artifacts rather than clinical or scientific advisors.

sections.heading: Appendix G Disagreement case studies
sections.text: To understand why judges disagree, we inspected training rollouts that the drop mask removed. The examples below come from the training logs of additional two-judge runs that pair GPT-4o-mini with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which we used because DeepSeek-V3.1 no longer returned token log-probabilities. Ratings are expected soft-Likert ratings on the 1–5 scale.

sections.heading: Contradicting an explicit rubric item.
sections.text: An ethics question asks whether a child’s refusal to donate bone marrow to her mother may be overridden. The rubric includes the essential item “Includes a clear statement such as ‘The child’s refusal to donate bone marrow should not be overridden.’ ” The response instead concludes that “the ethical decision to override the child’s refusal to donate bone marrow to save her mother’s life can be justified.” GPT-4o-mini rates it 4.99 despite the violation, while DeepSeek rates it 1.96.

sections.heading: Incomplete explanation.
sections.text: A physiology question has two essential rubric items: identifying “(D) Motilin” and mentioning the “Migrating Motor Complex (MMC).” The response correctly selects “D. Motilin” but never names the MMC in its explanation, missing the second item. GPT-4o-mini rates it 4.00 and DeepSeek 2.63. In both cases the rubric items are explicit, so the disagreement reflects how strictly each judge applies them rather than ambiguity in the rubric: direct violations can receive very different rewards, and incomplete explanations are penalized to different degrees. This pattern is systematic. Across 25,600 training rollouts from four two-judge runs, 25.35% were masked, and GPT-4o-mini gave the higher rating in 99.61% of masked rollouts, suggesting that it applies rubric items more leniently than DeepSeek.

sections.heading: Appendix I English-only HealthBench evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate on English HealthBench prompts only, to remove a possible confounder in grading. All HealthBench rubrics are written in English. In exploratory checks, English responses to Spanish prompts often received higher scores than Spanish responses, and translating rubrics into Spanish increased the average grade of Spanish responses. Multilingual comparisons may therefore partly reflect alignment between rubric and response language rather than response quality. Hisada et al. (2026) report a related effect for Japanese: grading Japanese responses against English rubrics can penalize appropriate responses, and many rubric criteria require localization. Evaluating multilingual robustness with localized rubrics is left to future work.

sections.heading: Appendix J Judge prompts
sections.text: We use two prompt families: a rubric-judge Likert-rating prompt (§ 3 , the primary RaR judge) and a plain pairwise-judge prompt (Appendix N baseline). Both use strict JSON- schema decoding so the judge output is constrained to a single integer rating (or single letter winner) with no rationale.

sections.heading: Rubric Likert judge (scale 1–5)
sections.text: System prompt. You are an expert evaluator. Given a user prompt, a generated response, and a list of quality rubrics, rate the overall quality of the response on a scale of 1 to 5 based on how well it satisfies the rubrics, where 1=very poor, 2=poor, 3=neutral, 4=good, 5=excellent. Respond with ONLY a valid JSON object of the form {"rating": <integer 1-5>} and nothing else (no code fences, no rationale, no additional fields). User prompt template. Given the following prompt, response, and rubrics, rate the overall quality of the response on a scale of 1 to 5 (1=very poor, 5=excellent). <prompt>{question}</prompt> <response>{response}</response> <rubrics>{rubric_text}</rubrics> Your JSON Evaluation (must be exactly {"rating": <integer 1-5>}): JSON schema. {"type": "object", "properties": {"rating": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 5}}, "required": ["rating"], "additionalProperties": false} The <rubrics> field is rendered as a flat newline-separated list of criterion descriptions (no weights, no category labels — the judge weighs them holistically). For the 1–10 scale used in gemds runs the anchors generalize to “1–2=very poor, 3–4=poor, 5–6=neutral, 7–8=good, 9–10=excellent” with the JSON schema bounded to maximum: 10 .

sections.heading: Pairwise (no-Likert) judge
sections.text: System prompt. You are an expert evaluator comparing two responses to a user prompt. Given a prompt, a list of quality rubrics, and two candidate responses (A and B), decide which response better satisfies the rubrics overall. You MUST pick exactly one, even if both are similar. Respond with ONLY a valid JSON object of the form {"winner": "A"} or {"winner": "B"} and nothing else (no code fences, no rationale, no additional fields). User prompt template. Given the following prompt, rubrics, and two responses (A and B), decide which response better satisfies the rubrics. <prompt>{question}</prompt> <rubrics>{rubric_text}</rubrics> <response_A>{response_a}</response_A> <response_B>{response_b}</response_B> Your JSON evaluation (must be exactly {"winner": "A"} or {"winner": "B"}): JSON schema. {"type": "object", "properties": {"winner": {"type": "string", "enum": ["A", "B"]}}, "required": ["winner"], "additionalProperties": false} The no-rubric ablation (Table 14 , “gem (no rubric)”) uses an identical prompt with the <rubrics> field and any “rubrics” wording removed; the judge then evaluates “accuracy, helpfulness, depth, and clarity” implicitly.

Anne Harrington 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Trevor Darrell Yutong Bai Affiliation: UC Berkeley Affiliation: {liu.michael, anneko, trevordarrell, yutongbai}@berkeley.edu Abstract Rubrics as Rewards (RaR) extends reinforcement learning to non-verifiable domains by using an LLM judge to score responses against a structured rubric. Prior work has focused on improving the rubric or strengthening the single judge, with comparatively little attention to how different single or multiple judges might be used during RaR training. We first show that judge identity alone produces a substantial spread in scores when training Qwen3-4B-Base on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science across five frontier and open-weight judges. Building on this, we propose RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a novel judge ensemble strategy for RaR with two mechanisms: a soft-Likert reward that uses judge logprobs to weight more confident judges more heavily, and a drop-on-disagreement mask that excludes high-disagreement rollouts from the GRPO update. We find that this design is critical: while a naive average of judge scores fails to outperform the best single judge, RaRE outperforms every single-judge RaR variant on both HealthBench and GPQA Diamond, with per-theme analysis showing that it inherits the complementary strengths of its constituent judges. Our findings establish judge ensembling as a compelling axis for improving RaR. 1 1 1 Project page: https://anneharrington.github.io/judging-the-judges/ 1 Introduction Rubrics as Rewards (RaR; Gunjal et al., 2025 ) is increasingly used in LLM post-training for learning on non-verifiable domains. Unlike Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which is standard for math and code ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , RaR enables training in more realistic settings where response quality might depend on multiple criteria that are not easily checked (such as completeness, style, and safety). RaR consists of two components: a structured, instance-specific rubric that encodes relevant criteria, and an LLM judge that scores each rollout against the rubric to produce a scalar reward. Following its success, subsequent work has explored in depth how to improve rubrics themselves; these include better offline construction ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , checklist-style scaffolding during rollouts ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and online rubric updates ( Rezaei et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . While the effect of the judge has been studied extensively at evaluation time, including work on judge ensembles ( Verga et al., 2024 ; Chan et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) , comparatively the impact of the judge during RaR training has been under-explored. To fill this gap, we evaluate the role of the judge model during RaR training more broadly. We train Qwen3-4B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science with the same strategy and rubrics as Gunjal et al. (2025) across 5 open and closed weight judging models. We show that varying judge identity alone in RaR produces a substantial spread in scores across both domains. Using our insights on the effect of the single judge model, we then develop RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a novel ensemble strategy to improve RaR. Rather than taking a naive average of judge scores, which we show fails to outperform the best single judge, RaRE targets two distinct sources of uncertainty. First, we introduce a soft-Likert reward to leverage intra-judge confidence: we use each judge’s logprobs to weight more confident judges more heavily in the ensemble. Second, we incorporate a drop-on-disagreement mask to leverage inter-judge disagreement: we exclude rollouts on which judges strongly disagree from the GRPO update. The two mechanisms can be used independently or composed. We validate RaRE on an ensemble of two judges, testing on the medicine and science domains using HealthBench ( Arora et al., 2025 ) and GPQA Diamond ( Rein et al., 2023 ) respectively. We find that our best RaRE configuration outperforms every single-judge RaR variant in both domains (0.364 vs. 0.339 best single judge on HealthBench; 0.412 vs. 0.406 best single judge on GPQA Diamond). Examining results by HealthBench theme, we find that RaRE consistently inherits the strengths of its judges, winning on all seven themes. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. A study of the judge in RaR training across five frontier and open-weight judges on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science, showing that judge identity alone substantially shifts policy quality. 2. RaRE, a novel ensemble method for RaR with two composable mechanisms: a soft-Likert reward that reads judge logprobs to recover confidence-weighted ratings, and a drop-on-disagreement mask that excludes high-disagreement rollouts from the GRPO update. 3. Empirical results showing that RaRE outperforms single-judge RaR variants in both medicine and science, with per-theme analysis revealing that it inherits complementary strengths of its judges, unlike a naive ensemble approach. 2 Related Work RL with verifiable rewards. Recent gains on math and code use deterministic checks (e.g., calculators, compilers) as the reward signal ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , typically optimized with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . These checks do not exist for open-ended domains such as medical or scientific ( Su et al., 2025 ) . Rubric-based rewards. Rubrics-as-Rewards ( Gunjal et al., 2025 ) and similar work ( Viswanathan et al., 2026 ) replace the binary verifier with an LLM judge that scores a candidate against a structured rubric, converting a fuzzy preference target into a scalar reward. Subsequent work has focused almost entirely on the rubric side: better offline construction ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , checklist-style scaffolding during rollouts ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , online rubric updates ( Rezaei et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , and causally grounded rubrics for robust reward modeling ( Srivastava et al., 2026 ) . Concurrent work ( Mahmoud et al., 2026 ) also uses multiple judges in the RaR setting, but as a multi-judge evaluation panel for detecting reward hacking, while RaRE uses the judge ensemble as the training signal itself. Across these works, the training judge model is consistently treated as a fixed implementation detail, usually a single model. Our work holds the rubric fixed and treats the judge itself as the design variable, complementary to all of the above. LLM-as-a-judge and verification. LLM-as-a-judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) has become the dominant evaluation paradigm, with growing emphasis on structured or rubric-conditioned grading ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Hashemi et al., 2024 ) . Recent reliability studies ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ; Kwok et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) show that single judges exhibit substantial position bias, length bias, and inter-seed variance. Our results in § 4.2 extend this diagnosis from evaluation to optimization: judge choice meaningfully affects the trained policy even with a fixed rubric. Judge ensembles. The closest prior work is Panel-of-LLM-evaluators ( Verga et al., 2024 ) , which mean-pools or majority-votes across a panel of smaller judges and shows that the panel outperforms a single large judge on evaluation while reducing intra-model bias. ChatEval ( Chan et al., 2024 ) explores a debate-based variant, and similar work ( Feng et al., 2025 ) finds that panel-based judging improves preference consistency. To our knowledge, all of this literature treats judge ensembles as an evaluation-time mechanism. RaRE instead uses a judge ensemble inside the RL training loop as the reward signal, with mechanisms (§ 3.1.2 , § 3.1.3 ) that use inter-judge spread as part of the training signal rather than only as a diagnostic. 3 Methods Notation. Five candidate single-judge configurations span proprietary, open-weight, and small-model regimes: gpt-4o-mini ( OpenAI, 2024 ) , DeepSeek-V3.1 ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ) , Gemini-2.5-flash-lite ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-235B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and gpt-oss-120b ( OpenAI et al., 2025 ) . All judges share the same rubric and same Likert-rating prompt template (Appendix J ). Soft-Likert (Eq. 7 ) requires the endpoint to return top_logprobs . We queried logprobs for the two judges used in our soft-Likert ensemble experiments (gpt-4o-mini and DeepSeek-V3.1); Gemini does not expose this in its API. All judges were run with no thinking or low effort reasoning when applicable. Training. We train on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science ( Gunjal et al., 2025 ) with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) using G = 8 G{=}8 generations per prompt and per-group reward normalization. Varying the judge under a fixed rubric produces a ∼ \sim 4.3 pp spread in HealthBench score across five judges. This spread is greater than the gap between Qwen3-4B-Base and the lowest single-judge RaR run. Prior RaR work has focused almost exclusively on improving the rubric, treating the judge as fixed. Our results suggest that the judge side carries comparable signal and deserves comparable attention. Ensembles win by combining complementary judges, not by averaging. We might expect a judge ensemble to smooth out variance from any single judge, with the ensemble converging toward the strongest judge. We do not find this. RaRE consistently improves on HealthBench themes beyond either of its two judges individually (Figure 4 ), suggesting that the gain comes from combining the judges’ non-overlapping strengths, rather than from selecting the stronger judge. Naive averaging does not extract this gain: the mean of judges’ ratings averages their individual scores and does not outperform the best single judge. The gain only appears once we filter high-disagreement rollouts. Disagreement filtering is the most impactful mechanism. Across our ablations, the drop-on-disagreement mask contributes the most. Adding it to the naive Gemini+DeepSeek mean ensemble lifts the score by + 4.0 +4.0 pp (0.307 to 0.347); removing it from the DeepSeek+4o-mini soft+drop configuration costs 3.4 3.4 pp (0.364 to 0.330). The soft-Likert reward provides additional gain when composed with the mask, but on its own does not outperform the best single judge on HealthBench. The broader LLM-as-a-verifier literature ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ; Kwok et al., 2026 ) reports a similar finding in the evaluation setting, where explicit disagreement filtering matters more than the choice of any single judge. Our results extend this from evaluation to training. Relation to concurrent and complementary work. Two recent directions are complementary to ours. Online rubric updates ( Rezaei et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) reduce reward-signal variance by improving rubric content during training; we reduce it by improving judge aggregation. The two operate on different parts of the RaR pipeline and should compose, though we leave that combination to future work. Concurrent work by Mahmoud et al. (2026) also uses multiple judges in the RaR setting, but in the opposite direction: they train against a single verifier and use a cross-family panel of three frontier judges to diagnose reward hacking, while we use multiple judges to produce the training signal. The two contributions are independent and could be combined, with RaRE serving as the training-time signal and their panel as the evaluation-time check. 6 Conclusion We proposed RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), combining a soft-Likert confidence-aggregation reward with a drop-on-disagreement mask, which outperforms every single-judge RaR variant on both HealthBench and GPQA-Diamond. Our results suggest RaRE’s gains arise from combining complementary judge strengths through confidence and disagreement aggregation. Limitations Due to limited compute, our experiments are restricted to a single base policy (Qwen3-4B-Base) evaluated on two domains: HealthBench (medicine) and GPQA Diamond (science), so our findings may not transfer to other policy families, model scales, or other domains. We mitigate this with per-theme and per-category breakdowns and extensive ablations, but broader validation is left to future work. We evaluate HealthBench with GPT-4o-mini, following the convention established by Arora et al. (2025) and Gunjal et al. (2025) , which may introduce evaluation-judge bias since it is also used as a training judge. To test whether this overlap affects our results, we regrade policy responses with GLM-5.3-Flash, a judge from a different model family (Appendix D ). Relative rankings remain similar, and RaRE ranks first under both judges. A larger multi-judge evaluation panel, such as the one used by Mahmoud et al. (2026) , would provide additional robustness against evaluation-judge bias; our GPQA Diamond results, which use verifier-style evaluation rather than an LLM judge, partially address this concern. RaRE’s improvement on GPQA Diamond compared to single-judge RaR is not statistically significant across 5 training seeds. Running additional seeds could help tighten confidence intervals and allow for a more definitive comparison, which we leave to future work due to compute constraints. When applying RaRE’s drop-on-disagreement mask, we discard the dropped rollouts entirely rather than extracting any partial signal from them. Initial exploratory attempts in this direction (Appendix O ) did not yield any improvement over our baseline methods, but further exploration is left to future work. Finally, RaRE depends on inter-judge disagreement as a signal. When judges largely agree, RaRE provides little additional signal beyond a single judge; a more diverse judge pool could expand the regime where ensembling helps. Ethical Considerations Our work studies how judge selection and judge ensembling affect rubric-based RL training, with the goal of making the reward signal more reliable. Because the resulting policies are trained against LLM-judge rewards, they inherit biases of the judges used: RaRE reduces idiosyncratic per-judge bias but does not eliminate biases shared across judges, and the drop-on-disagreement filter removes precisely those rollouts where judges disagree most, which could exclude cases where a single judge correctly flags a safety-relevant issue that others miss. We therefore encourage practitioners who deploy ensemble-trained policies, particularly in health or scientific contexts, to audit them separately for these biases rather than treat ensembling as a substitute for evaluation, and we treat the models in this work as research artifacts rather than clinical or scientific advisors. Appendix G Disagreement case studies To understand why judges disagree, we inspected training rollouts that the drop mask removed. The examples below come from the training logs of additional two-judge runs that pair GPT-4o-mini with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which we used because DeepSeek-V3.1 no longer returned token log-probabilities. Ratings are expected soft-Likert ratings on the 1–5 scale. Contradicting an explicit rubric item. An ethics question asks whether a child’s refusal to donate bone marrow to her mother may be overridden. The rubric includes the essential item “Includes a clear statement such as ‘The child’s refusal to donate bone marrow should not be overridden.’ ” The response instead concludes that “the ethical decision to override the child’s refusal to donate bone marrow to save her mother’s life can be justified.” GPT-4o-mini rates it 4.99 despite the violation, while DeepSeek rates it 1.96. Incomplete explanation. A physiology question has two essential rubric items: identifying “(D) Motilin” and mentioning the “Migrating Motor Complex (MMC).” The response correctly selects “D. Motilin” but never names the MMC in its explanation, missing the second item. GPT-4o-mini rates it 4.00 and DeepSeek 2.63. In both cases the rubric items are explicit, so the disagreement reflects how strictly each judge applies them rather than ambiguity in the rubric: direct violations can receive very different rewards, and incomplete explanations are penalized to different degrees. This pattern is systematic. Across 25,600 training rollouts from four two-judge runs, 25.35% were masked, and GPT-4o-mini gave the higher rating in 99.61% of masked rollouts, suggesting that it applies rubric items more leniently than DeepSeek. Appendix I English-only HealthBench evaluation We evaluate on English HealthBench prompts only, to remove a possible confounder in grading. All HealthBench rubrics are written in English. In exploratory checks, English responses to Spanish prompts often received higher scores than Spanish responses, and translating rubrics into Spanish increased the average grade of Spanish responses. Multilingual comparisons may therefore partly reflect alignment between rubric and response language rather than response quality. Hisada et al. (2026) report a related effect for Japanese: grading Japanese responses against English rubrics can penalize appropriate responses, and many rubric criteria require localization. Evaluating multilingual robustness with localized rubrics is left to future work.
